records.title: Narrative entry

fields.event: Surfaced - commenced closing reference point at s/s on 1 M.E. No fighter protection. Between this time and 0913 when escorts arrived, 3 single Jap planes closed but headed away before we had to dive. Our formations in the distance seemed to deter them from attacking or perhaps they thought we were a straggler sampan. (Sampans were still in sight).

flags: '1 M.E.' (Bonsai; Qwen read 'l'). 'Sampans' typed 'Sampsns' (Qwen).

fields.event: Sighted first of 4 waves of our planes to attack and planes were in sight for the remainder of the day. At this time our fighter escorts had not arrived and the situation on the bridge was still tense as we did not know friend from foe at this time. Planes sighted during remainder of strike are not listed as plane contacts.

Large column of smoke and high flame sighted just on horizon bearing 307°T about 10 miles north of end of FORMOSA. Commenced closing on 4 engines thinking it was downed plane. At this time, our escorts finally showed up and informed us it was a sampan damaged by our planes. Commenced patrolling station slowly under our fighter coverage. Tension on bridge had eased slightly. The island was now almost obscured by fog and mist and we could see nothing of the show.

records.title: F6F with smoking engine coming down

fields.event: Sighted 5 F6F fighters headed for us, one plane trailing black smoke, Were notified by escorts he was going to land close aboard.

records.title: Lt(jg) McGuire picked up

fields.event: Plane made flat landing in water 300 yds. dead ahead, broke in two and apparently sank immediately. Pilot was then seen in water as we approached at frantic speed. Pilot was struggling weakly, apparently overcome by shock, gas and oil fumes, and salt water. Lieut(jg) C.J. ROBERTS dove into the water and swam a line to him and assisted him alongside. Picked up Lieutenant (jg) JOHN J. McGUIRE, U.S.N.R., #250542, of Squadron VF8 from U.S.S. BUNKER HILL, suffering from shock, shaken up, and weak, but without a scratch upon him. Notified his cohorts over VHF of his condition.

fields.narrative:
With range 4,000 yds., angle on the bow 90 port and torpedo run too great, commenced firing the bow tubes gambling on one of them having a long run. We were firing into the wind and sea. (Just prior to firing at the tanker, one escort had crossed our bow and we almost fired at him, all fish being set on 4 feet. We let him go by, however, and there was not time to change the depth settings back to greater depth). One torpedo broached all the way down the range: alerting the tanker who zigged left, toward us, swinging fast. We were swinging right and settled on course 270°T. The tanker headed across our stern on course 000°T at increased speed. All forward tubes had missed.

Commenced firing after tubes with range 1400 yds., angle on bow 90, course 000°T, speed 14 knots. 2 minutes later heard first torpedo hit. Raised scope and observed 2 more hits, all in stern which was obliterated by smoke and flying debris. Smoke cleared to show a portion of the stern gone. His screws stopped never to turn again. Fourth fish hit, but I was looking at an escort who had turned toward us with a zero angle on bow and a bone in his teeth, Retired to safer depth, 320 feet; where our inductions would be safer, and while passing 120 feet heard a tremendous explosion which was not a depth charge, and which rumbled and crackled for about 20 seconds to the accompaniment of heavy minor explosions. While going deep, 3 more escorts joined the chase, and as we hit 200', the first escort made a beautiful run and dropped a pattern over us followed by other escorts in quick succession. The 4th escort, presumably the AK, stayed off to the side apparently coaching. The encirclement method was employed, and we were boxed in very quickly. A 3 degree negative temperature gradient was found starting at 250 feet. Stayed at standard speed heading for escort who had made the last run. This course was into the wind and sea and away from the tanker, giving the SALMON a chance to get in and finish the tanker or AK. Slowed to 2/3 speed, which was maintained throughout the evasion tactics. During the next hour, 78 depth charges were dropped, all pretty close, screws were heard on at least two runs passing overhead, once close aboard down the stbd side, and the rest astern.

records.title: Depth-charged after the tanker attack

fields.event: The enemy counter-measures encountered on the attack of 30 October were very good during the first phase. Immediately after the first torpedo explosion, one escort made a beautiful run directly over us and dropped about 7 charges overhead as we passed 200 feet helping us to go deeper, and a second escort dropped a pattern overhead as we passed 300 feet. Settled at 320 feet. Escorts continued runs on us until a total of 70 charges were dropped, each pattern falling progressively farther astern. Immediately after the first pattern, a string of about 20 light explosions were heard at about 1 second intervals. The encirclement method was used with 3 escorts circling and pinging and one listening. We held 2/3 speed and a southeasterly course between changes of course to put tail to attacking escort, and after two hours, put escorts astern. S.E. course was into wind and sea. Negative temperature gradient was 3° with a good layer at 320 feet. Predicted echo range was 1700 yds. at 320 feet. Course drew escorts away from crippled tanker, but evasion tactics were too successful as escorts were back at tanker at 1915 in time to detect the SALMON making an approach. These escorts had no radar, however, radar was used by the heavy ships encountered on 26 October.

fields.event: Escorts were falling slowly astern, our course 150°T, so made reload and started up only to have one escort start toward us.
Started up again.

Surfaced. 3 pips on radar at 15,000 yds., bearing 300°T. We were in the moon slick but luckily had a bad horizon behind us. Headed north with two engines on charge and two on propulsion to get in position for another attack if opportunity presented itself. Antenna trunk was flooded out, so we had only the S.D. radar mast, and sent out serial four to COMSUBPAC, and reports to other submarines on wolfpack frequency. Received no reply. During this time, we were getting snatches of messages showing that SALMON, SILVERSIDES, and STERLET were making a coordinated attack. Held off closing to get more dope on their positions.

Saw gunfire bearing 180°T. Unable to raise SALMON or SILVERSIDES. Commenced closing gun flashes. Picked up S.J. radar interference ahead. Challenged on S.J., but got no reply. Decided to go around this stranger, but he was between us and the gun flashes and it was a long process. This sub was later identified as the STERLET proceeding towards target. STERLET reported putting 4 hits in tanker we had hit. Why it didn't sink before, with that tremendous explosion, we will never know. Sent latest dope to COMSUBPAC and all submarines.

The SPR-SPA has certainly proved its worth. It has, on 2 separate occasions on this patrol, given advance notice and identification of the arrival of major task forces, one Jap and one friendly, as well as numerous plane contacts. records.title: Joint gun action on a net tender; no hits

fields.event: Had closed target to 8,000 yds. He was a small net tender and had been running away during our approach at approximately 12 kts. Commenced firing with STERLET and SILVERSIDES, with SILVERSIDES astern of target, STERLET on target's stbd. quarter and TRIGGER on port quarter. Target commenced maneuvering radically, and returning fire when range was 7,000 yards, and scored several straddles on us. At 5,600 yards, heavy straddles were all around. Maneuvered to keep out of his range which appeared to be around 6,800 yds., and continued firing with 4". The 4" gun shooting was heartbreaking. Using radar ranges and high periscope spotting, we scored many near misses, several times splashing him with water, but we could not hit.
